answers.text:
This is the term Seth introduces for the specific philosophical position he spends the rest of the essay arguing against. As he defines it right in this passage: consciousness is a matter of computation—more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. He's careful to flag that this is an assumption, not an established fact, even though it usually goes unnoticed as one: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.

The stakes of the term are made explicit in the same breath: if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with. So this single phrase names the load-bearing premise underneath the entire "conscious AI" debate—if consciousness just is a certain kind of computation, then a sufficiently sophisticated program could in principle be conscious, no matter what it's made of. Everything that follows in the essay (the arguments that brains aren't really computers, that other non-computational dynamics may matter, that life itself may be necessary, and that simulating something isn't the same as creating it) is Seth's case for why this specific assumption is shakier than people tend to realize.

It's worth distinguishing this from the more general idea of "functionalism" in philosophy of mind, which the article addresses later: the looser claim that mental properties depend on a system's functional organization, without specifying that the relevant organization must be computational in Turing's specific sense. One of the factors contributing to confusion in this area has been a tendency to conflate the rather liberal position of functionalism-in-general, since functional organization can include many things, with the very specific claim of computational functionalism, which implies that the type of organization that matters is computational and which in turn is often assumed to relate to Turing-style algorithms in particular. So computational functionalism is the narrow, strong version — the one Seth thinks is doing unexamined work in most claims that AI could become conscious.

answers.asked: This assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all.
answers.text:
Computational functionalism is the term Seth introduces just before this sentence for the assumption underlying the whole idea of conscious AI: that consciousness is a matter of computation — more specifically, that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise.

The point of the sentence you've selected is about how invisible this assumption has become. Because so much of modern thinking about minds and machines takes the "mind as software, brain as hardware" picture for granted, people treat it as simply obvious rather than as a contestable philosophical position. Seth is flagging this as a rhetorical move he's about to make: he's going to spend the rest of the essay excavating this buried premise and arguing against it — "if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with." So this line is the hinge of the essay's structure — everything that follows (the four arguments about brains not being computers, other non-computational "games in town," biological naturalism, and simulation vs. instantiation) is an attempt to make this hidden assumption visible and then test whether it survives scrutiny.

Outside the article, computational functionalism is a real position in philosophy of mind, most associated with thinkers like Hilary Putnam and later defended in various forms by people like David Chalmers (who appears later in the essay). It's the view that what makes something have a particular mental state is its functional or causal role, not the physical material it's made of — meaning, in principle, a mind could run on silicon just as well as on neurons, provided the computational structure is preserved. Seth's target throughout the essay is specifically the stronger, narrower version of this claim: that Turing-style digital computation in particular is what would be sufficient, which is why he spends so much time later distinguishing "computation" in the strict Turing sense from broader notions of functional organization.

answers.asked: What does "computational functionalism" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
Computational functionalism is the assumption, as the article puts it, that consciousness is a matter of computation — that implementing the right kind of computation, or information processing, is sufficient for consciousness to arise. Seth stresses that this is usually treated as obvious rather than as a premise: this assumption, which philosophers call computational functionalism, is so deeply ingrained that it can be difficult to recognize it as an assumption at all [spya-wepmnr].

It matters because Seth's whole case against conscious AI is really a case against this one assumption. He says outright that if it's wrong, as I think it may be, then real artificial consciousness is fully off the table, at least for the kinds of AI we're familiar with [spya-wepmnr]. The four arguments that follow — brains not being computers, the existence of non-computational "other games in town," the possibility that life itself matters, and the gap between simulation and instantiation — are all aimed at this target. He later ties them back together explicitly: Computational functionalism — the claim that (algorithmic) computation is sufficient for consciousness — is a very strong assumption that looks increasingly shaky as the many and deep differences between brains and (standard digital) computers come into view [spya-ymbpwn].

The assumption also does hidden work elsewhere in the essay. Whole-brain emulation and mind-uploading schemes only make sense if it's true, since the prospect of instantiating consciousness through some kind of whole-brain emulation, at some arbitrarily high level of detail, already assumes that computational functionalism is true [spya-pbcr03]. And Seth points out that even Bostrom's simulation hypothesis quietly depends on it: it is telling that he notes one necessary assumption, and then just takes it as a given… the assumption that "a computer running a suitable program would be conscious" [spya-xdy4fe]. So the term functions in the piece as the hinge premise that most "conscious AI is coming" arguments lean on without ever defending — and Seth's essay is essentially an extended argument that this hinge is weaker than it looks, though, as he says himself, nothing in what I've said rules out the possibility of artificial consciousness altogether [spya-rn8y3y].

Autopoiesis is the term the article just introduced a moment earlier, in the sentence describing how even a single neuron is "busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence." The word itself, as the article notes, comes "from the Greek for 'self-production.'" The article treats it as "arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems."

Beyond what the article says, the term was coined in the early 1970s by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to distinguish living systems from mere machines. An autopoietic system is one that continuously produces and repairs its own components and its own boundary (like a cell manufacturing the very membrane and molecules that keep it alive), so that the system is, in effect, the process that makes itself. This is contrasted with "allopoietic" systems, like a factory or a computer, which produce something other than themselves — a car factory makes cars, not more factories.

Seth is reaching for this concept precisely because it marks the point where the "brain as computer" metaphor starts to strain: a computer's hardware doesn't need to continuously regenerate itself in order to keep computing, but a neuron's very existence depends on this ongoing self-making activity, which is one of the reasons he goes on to argue that brains can't be cleanly split into hardware and software the way computers can.

answers.asked: (This process is called autopoiesis, from the Greek for “self-production.” Autopoiesis is arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems.)
answers.text:
The word "autopoiesis" comes from the Greek for self-production, and it's a term coined in the 1970s by the Chilean biologists Humberto Maturana and Francisco Varela to describe what they saw as the defining feature of living systems: a living thing isn't just a static structure but a process that continuously builds and rebuilds its own components and its own boundary, using its own activity to keep itself in existence. A cell, for instance, is constantly breaking down and replacing its own molecules, repairing its membrane, and regenerating the very machinery that does all that repairing — it produces itself, rather than being produced and left alone the way a machine is manufactured once and then simply run.

In the passage, Seth uses this idea right after describing a single neuron as "a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence" — that description of self-maintenance is exactly what autopoiesis names. The point feeds into his larger argument against treating brains as computers: a silicon chip just sits there executing instructions, but a neuron is simultaneously the thing computing and the thing keeping itself alive, so you can't cleanly peel apart "what it does" (its function) from "what it is" (its physical, self-sustaining existence) the way you can with software and hardware. That inseparability is one of his four reasons for doubting that consciousness could ever be captured by digital computation alone.

answers.asked: What does "autopoiesis" mean here, and why does it matter to the argument?
answers.text:
In this piece, "autopoiesis" (from the Greek for "self-production") names the fact that even a single living neuron is a spectacularly complicated biological machine, busy maintaining its own integrity and regenerating the conditions and material basis for its own continued existence, a process the author calls autopoiesis, arguably a defining and distinctive characteristic of living systems [spya-cf8rt8].

It matters to the argument because it's the basis for Seth's first case against "computational functionalism" — the assumption that the right computation is enough for consciousness. He uses it to say that, unlike in a computer, brains are the kinds of things for which it is difficult, and likely impossible, to separate what they do from what they are [spya-zw2m7u]. Because a neuron isn't just running an algorithm but is constantly rebuilding its own physical substrate, the idea of the brain as a meat-based Turing machine rests precisely on a sharp separation between what brains do and what they are — a separation that autopoiesis undermines — so the mathematical marriage of convenience between brains and algorithms starts to fall apart [spya-p4vmm0].

The concept resurfaces later in his positive proposal (biological naturalism): he links the drive to stay alive reaching into the molecular furnaces of metabolism, where prediction-error minimization becomes inseparable from the materiality of life itself, drawing a mathematical line from the self-producing, autopoietic nature of biological material to the perceptual best-guessing behind conscious experience [spya-vys3vj]. So autopoiesis functions as the concrete biological detail that grounds two of his four arguments: it's evidence that brains resist the software/hardware split computers rely on, and it's the thread connecting "being alive" to "being conscious" in his own account of why life might matter for consciousness.
